records.name: Osei Tutu I, founder of Asante
records.scaleNote: Founder of the state whose wars later made it one of the Gold Coast's main suppliers of captives; numbers for his own reign are not documented.
records.origins: Ruler of the small Kwaman state from about 1680, he worked with the priest Okomfo Anokye to unite the Akan states of the Kumasi area around the Golden Stool.
records.role_summary: He led the Asante alliance that defeated its overlord Denkyira at Feyiase in 1701 and set up the institutions of the Asante Empire. His wars, and those of his successors, produced captives sold to Dutch and English traders on the coast.

roleDetail.d: Defeated Denkyira in 1701 and ruled as first Asantehene until about 1717.
Asante's expansion fed captives into the Gold Coast trade with the Dutch at Elmina and the English at Cape Coast.

records.legacy: The Golden Stool he founded is still the symbol of Asante unity; his successor on it today is Otumfuo Osei Tutu II.

legacyDetail.d: The stool remains the centre of Asante kingship in Kumasi.

connections.label: Asante war captives sold at the coast

lineage.name: Okomfo Anokye
lineage.note: Chief priest credited with bringing down the Golden Stool and codifying Asante law.

lineage.name: Opoku Ware I
lineage.note: Second Asantehene, who greatly expanded the empire.

lineage.name: Osei Bonsu
lineage.note: Asantehene at the height of Asante power.

lineage.name: Otumfuo Osei Tutu II
lineage.note: Present Asantehene, who took the regnal name of the founder.

records.today: The Asante kingdom survives within Ghana, and Otumfuo Nana Osei Tutu II, enstooled in 1999, holds the Golden Stool. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Akitoye, Oba of Lagos
records.scaleNote: A Lagos ruler during the illegal-trade era; he signed the 1852 abolition treaty but let the trade continue, per his Wikipedia biography.
records.origins: A son of Oba Ologun Kutere, he became Oba of Lagos in 1841 but was overthrown by his nephew Kosoko in 1845 and fled to Badagry and Abeokuta.
records.role_summary: In exile he allied with the anti-slavery cause to win British backing. Britain bombarded Lagos in 1851 and restored him; on 1 January 1852 he signed the treaty abolishing the slave trade, yet he allowed Madam Tinubu and others to keep trading captives covertly.

roleDetail.d: Reinstated after the 1851 Reduction of Lagos.
Signed the Anglo-Lagos treaty outlawing the slave trade on 1 January 1852.
Granted Madam Tinubu commercial privileges and land at today's Tinubu Square.

records.legacy: His son Dosunmu succeeded him, and his line kept the Lagos throne. The first Eyo procession is said to have been held for his funeral.

legacyDetail.d: Lagos tradition holds that the first Eyo procession commemorated his death.

lineage.name: Ologun Kutere
lineage.note: Founder of the dominant Lagos royal line.

lineage.name: Osinlokun and Adele
lineage.note: Brothers who reigned as Oba before him.

lineage.name: Madam Tinubu
lineage.note: Widow of his brother Adele and his political ally.

lineage.name: Kosoko
lineage.note: Overthrew him in 1845.

lineage.name: Dosunmu
lineage.note: Ceded Lagos to Britain in 1861.

lineage.name: Ibikunle Akitoye
lineage.note: Later Oba of Lagos from his line.

records.today: His descendants through Dosunmu remain central to the Lagos royal house; the present Oba of Lagos is Rilwan Akiolu (since 2003). Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: William Dappa Pepple I, King of Bonny
records.scaleNote: King of Bonny in the last decades of its slave exports and the shift to palm oil; volumes in his reign are not separately documented.
records.origins: A member of the Perekule (Pepple) royal house, he came to the throne of Bonny in 1830 when the port was still exporting captives.
records.role_summary: He signed anti-slave-trade agreements with Britain under naval pressure while Bonny moved into palm oil. Rivalries between the royal trading houses led Britain to depose and exile him in 1854; he was restored in 1861 and ruled until his death in 1866.

roleDetail.d: Reigned as Bonny moved from the slave trade to palm oil.
Deposed by the British in 1854 and restored in 1861 with the help of Chief Omoni Jack Brown.

records.legacy: His son George Oruigbiji Pepple succeeded him, and the Pepple house still provides Bonny's king.

legacyDetail.d: The present Amanyanabo, Edward Asimini William Dappa Pepple III, bears his name.

sources.label: Victorian Web — King William Dappa Pepple

connections.label: Anna Pepple House chief under his successors

lineage.name: Opubo the Great
lineage.note: Predecessor during Bonny's slave-trade peak.

lineage.name: George Oruigbiji Pepple (Perekule VII)
lineage.note: English-educated king from 1866.

lineage.name: Edward Asimini William Dappa Pepple III
lineage.note: Present king of Grand Bonny.

records.today: The Pepple dynasty still reigns in Grand Bonny under King Edward Asimini William Dappa Pepple III (Perekule XI). Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Eyo Honesty II of Creek Town
records.scaleNote: Leading Efik trader of Creek Town; Old Calabar kept exporting captives until about 1840, after which he traded palm oil.
records.origins: Born Eyo Eyo Nsa into a prominent Efik trading family, son of Eyo Nsa ('Willy Honesty'), he said he began poor and built his wealth by trading with European ships.
records.role_summary: As ruler of Creek Town from 1835 he was one of the richest traders in Old Calabar, active as slave exports ended around 1840 and palm oil took over. He invited Presbyterian missionaries (Hope Waddell's mission arrived in 1846) and worked to end twin-killing and the killing of slaves at funerals.

roleDetail.d: Built a fortune trading with European ships before and after abolition.
Helped invite the Presbyterian mission to Calabar in 1846.
Opposed twin-killing and the sacrifice of enslaved people at funerals.

records.legacy: His son Eyo Honesty III succeeded him, and the Eyo house remains one of the Efik royal houses of Calabar.

legacyDetail.d: Creek Town remains a seat of the Eyo royal house.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Timeline of Old Calabar history

lineage.name: Eyo Nsa ('Willy Honesty')
lineage.note: Prominent Efik trader of his day.

lineage.name: Esien Ekpe Oku (Iyamba I)
lineage.note: Through his mother, Princess Inyang Esien Ekpe.

lineage.name: Eyo Honesty III
lineage.note: Eldest son, who succeeded him.

records.today: The Eyo house remains one of the Efik royal houses of Creek Town and Calabar. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Adandozan, King of Dahomey
records.scaleNote: Dahomey's slave exports were depressed during his reign; he raided the Mahi for captives with little success.
records.origins: He succeeded his father Agonglo in 1797 while still young, under a regent until 1804.
records.role_summary: He tried to revive slave exports by raiding the Mahi to the north and disrupting rival ports, sent embassies to Portugal (1804) and the British at Cape Coast, and later promoted agriculture. He quarrelled with Francisco Félix de Souza, who backed his brother Ghezo's coup in 1818.

roleDetail.d: Raided the Mahi to supply the slave trade, largely without success.
Sent ambassadors to Portugal in 1804.
Deposed by Ghezo with de Souza's help and erased from official king lists.

records.legacy: Ghezo and Glele painted him as a cruel usurper and removed him from official history. A 2018 conference at the University of Abomey-Calavi marked 'two hundred years of ostracism'.

legacyDetail.d: Beninese scholars have re-examined his reign.

connections.label: imprisoned de Souza; overthrown with his help

lineage.name: Agonglo
lineage.note: King assassinated in 1797.

lineage.name: Ghezo
lineage.note: Deposed him in 1818.

lineage.name: Francisco Félix de Souza
lineage.note: Trader he imprisoned, who then helped overthrow him.

records.today: No individual descendants are named here. His name has been partly restored by Beninese historians; members of the royal lineages carry no guilt for the kingdom's slave trade.

records.name: Béhanzin, King of Dahomey
records.scaleNote: Reigned after the Atlantic slave trade had largely ended; Dahomey still relied on war captives and enslaved labour at home.
records.origins: Born Kondo, a son of King Glele, he took the throne in January 1890 after his father's death.
records.role_summary: He led Dahomey against France in the Franco-Dahomean wars. French propaganda used the killing of captives at the Annual Customs to justify conquest. Defeated in 1894, he was exiled to Martinique and later Algeria.

roleDetail.d: Ruled 1890–1894 and resisted French conquest.
Dahomey's state still depended on captives and enslaved labour, which France used as propaganda.

records.legacy: He died in exile in 1906; his remains were later returned to Abomey. Royal objects taken by France are in the Musée du Quai Branly and at the centre of restitution debates.

legacyDetail.d: His throne and statues taken in 1892 are central to Benin's restitution claims.

lineage.name: Glele
lineage.note: Previous king.

lineage.name: Agoli-agbo
lineage.note: Installed by the French.

lineage.name: Georges Collinet Béhanzin (Dada Dèwènondè Gbéhanzin)
lineage.note: Member of his line chosen as king of Dahomey in 2022.

records.today: In February 2022 Georges Collinet Béhanzin was enthroned at Abomey as Dada Dèwènondè Gbéhanzin, chosen by agreement among the rival royal lineages. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi
records.scaleNote: Founder of the dynasty that later built the Zanzibar slave economy; his own role in East African slaving is not quantified.
records.origins: A governor of Sohar during the Omani civil war, he led resistance to the Persian occupation and was elected imam about 1749.
records.role_summary: He founded the Al Bu Said dynasty and restored Oman's position in the Gulf and Indian Ocean trade, including claims on the Swahili coast that his descendants turned into a slave-and-clove empire.

roleDetail.d: First Al Bu Said ruler, c.1749–1783.
Rebuilt Oman's trade and navy.

legacyDetail.d: Sultan Haitham bin Tariq (since 2020) is the fifteenth ruler of the dynasty.

connections.label: Omani claims on the Swahili coast

lineage.name: Sultan bin Ahmad
lineage.note: Ruled Oman and fathered Sayyid Saʿīd.

lineage.name: Sayyid Saʿīd bin Sultan
lineage.note: Moved the court to Zanzibar.

lineage.name: Haitham bin Tariq
lineage.note: Present Sultan of Oman.

records.today: The dynasty he founded rules Oman today under Sultan Haitham bin Tariq. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Majid bin Said, first Sultan of Zanzibar
records.scaleNote: Ruled Zanzibar at the height of its slave market in the 1860s, when tens of thousands of captives a year passed through, per historians of the trade.
records.origins: A son of Sayyid Saʿīd, he took Zanzibar and the East African coast when his father's realm was divided in 1856.
records.role_summary: His sultanate's revenue rested on the slave market, slave-worked clove plantations and customs on ivory and captives. He survived a coup attempt by his brother Barghash in 1859, accepted the 1861 Canning Award separating Zanzibar from Oman, and began building Dar es Salaam.

roleDetail.d: Ruled Zanzibar 1856–1870 after the split with Oman.
His treasury depended on taxes on the slave and ivory trades.

records.legacy: His brother Barghash succeeded him and was forced to close the slave market in 1873.

legacyDetail.d: He began building the town that became Tanzania's largest city.

connections.label: customs farmed by Jairam Shivji's firm

lineage.name: Sayyid Saʿīd bin Sultan
lineage.note: Divided his realm between sons.

lineage.name: Thuwaini bin Said
lineage.note: Ruled Oman.

lineage.name: Barghash bin Said
lineage.note: Attempted a coup in 1859; succeeded in 1870.

records.today: The Zanzibar sultanate he founded ended in the 1964 revolution. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Sefu bin Hamid
records.scaleNote: Son and lieutenant of Tippu Tip who ran his father's slave-and-ivory network in the eastern Congo; numbers undocumented.
records.origins: The son of Tippu Tip, he grew up in his father's trading world and took charge of his interests in the eastern Congo.
records.role_summary: After Tippu Tip left the Congo, Sefu was one of the strongmen who held power there. In 1892 he attacked Belgian ivory traders, starting the Congo Arab war against the Congo Free State; he was killed in October 1893.

roleDetail.d: Ran Tippu Tip's network from Kasongo.
His 1892 attack began the war in which he was killed in 1893.

records.legacy: His defeat ended Zanzibari power in the eastern Congo and opened it to Leopold's regime.

legacyDetail.d: The war was used by Leopold's state to present its conquest as anti-slavery.

lineage.name: Tippu Tip
lineage.note: Leading Zanzibari slave and ivory trader.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced.

records.name: Usman dan Fodio
records.scaleNote: His jihad founded the Sokoto Caliphate, which became one of the largest slave societies of the 19th century; jihad captives were also sold south to the coast.
records.origins: A Fulani Muslim scholar from Gobir, son of the scholar Muhammad Fodio, he preached from 1774 and built a reformist community at Degel.
records.role_summary: He criticised the Hausa kings for enslaving Muslims, overtaxation and injustice, but the jihad he led from 1804 took many non-Muslim captives, and the caliphate came to depend on enslaved labour and raiding. He was proclaimed Commander of the Faithful and died at Sokoto in 1817.

roleDetail.d: Led the 1804–08 jihad that overthrew the Hausa kingdoms.
He condemned enslaving Muslims, yet the jihad and caliphate produced vast numbers of captives.
Wrote widely, including 'Nur al-Ibad'.

records.legacy: His tomb in Sokoto is a place of pilgrimage, and his descendants hold the sultanate.

legacyDetail.d: The Sultan of Sokoto, Sa'adu Abubakar (since 2006), is his descendant and spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of sultans of Sokoto

connections.label: Hausa and Yoruba Muslim captives in Bahia

lineage.name: Muhammad Fodio
lineage.note: Islamic scholar who taught him at Degel.

lineage.name: Abdullahi dan Fodio
lineage.note: Scholar and vizier who ruled the western half of the caliphate.

lineage.name: Muhammad Bello
lineage.note: First Sultan of Sokoto.

lineage.name: Nana Asmaʾu
lineage.note: Poet and scholar.

lineage.name: Sa'adu Abubakar
lineage.note: Present Sultan of Sokoto.

records.today: His descendants hold the Sokoto Sultanate; Sa'adu Abubakar has been Sultan since 2006. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi
records.scaleNote: Effective ruler of Bornu when it exported captives across the Sahara to Fezzan and Tripoli; numbers not documented for his rule.
records.origins: An Islamic scholar who had studied in the Middle East, he returned to Bornu as Fulani jihadists attacked it around 1808.
records.role_summary: He drove back the Fulani forces with a small band of students and mercenaries, and the Sayfawa mai Dunama IX rewarded him with power. He became Bornu's real ruler, founded Kukawa, and presided over a state that raided its southern neighbours and sold captives north across the Sahara.

roleDetail.d: Repelled the Sokoto jihad from about 1808.
His Bornu sent captives north via Murzuq to Tripoli.

records.legacy: His son Umar ended the Sayfawa line in 1846; the al-Kanemi shehus still rule Borno.

legacyDetail.d: Abubakar Ibn Umar Garbai El-Kanemi has been Shehu since 2009.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Abubakar ibn Umar Garba el-Kanemi

lineage.name: Dunama IX Lefiami
lineage.note: Sayfawa king who gave him power.

lineage.name: Umar ibn Muhammad al-Amin
lineage.note: Ended the Sayfawa line.

lineage.name: Abubakar Ibn Umar Garbai El-Kanemi
lineage.note: Present Shehu of Borno.

records.today: The al-Kanemi line still provides the Shehu of Borno. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Isma'il Pasha, Khedive of Egypt
records.scaleNote: Ruled Egypt and Sudan while slave raiding in the White Nile and Bahr el Ghazal peaked; he also signed the 1877 Anglo-Egyptian slave-trade convention.
records.origins: A grandson of Muhammad ʿAlī, he became ruler of Egypt in 1863 and took the title of Khedive in 1867.
records.role_summary: He expanded Egyptian rule in Sudan and made the slave trader al-Zubayr a pasha and governor of Bahr el Ghazal, while also hiring Europeans such as Samuel Baker and Charles Gordon to suppress the trade. Heavy debts led Britain and France to have him removed in 1879.

roleDetail.d: Pushed Egyptian power deep into Sudan.
Granted the slave trader Zubayr titles and a governorship.
Employed Baker and Gordon against the trade, a contradiction historians stress.

records.legacy: Deposed in 1879, he died in exile in 1895; his dynasty ruled until 1953.

legacyDetail.d: Fuad II, the last king (1952–53), is his great-grandson.

lineage.name: Muhammad ʿAlī
lineage.note: Founder of the dynasty.

lineage.name: Ibrahim Pasha
lineage.note: General and briefly ruler of Egypt.

lineage.name: Zubayr Pasha
lineage.note: Slave trader he made governor.

lineage.name: Fuad II
lineage.note: Last King of Egypt and titular head of the dynasty.

records.today: The Muhammad Ali dynasty's monarchy was abolished in 1953; Fuad II is its senior member. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Thomas Corker (founder of the Caulkers)
records.scaleNote: Royal African Company agent at a slave-trading station; his personal volumes are not documented, but his descendants became a major trading clan.
records.origins: Born in Falmouth, Cornwall, son of a ship's doctor, he joined the Royal African Company as an apprentice at 14 and was sent to the Guinea coast.
records.role_summary: He became chief agent on York Island, a slave-trading centre on the Sherbro River, and married a daughter of a Sherbro chief, known to the English as Seniora Doll. He died in 1700, leaving two sons who inherited their mother's chiefdom.

roleDetail.d: Chief RAC agent at York Island, Sherbro.
His marriage into a Sherbro ruling house gave his sons land and chiefly rights.

records.legacy: His sons Robin and Stephen founded the Caulker dynasty of Sherbro chiefs and slave traders.

legacyDetail.d: The clan still keeps oral and written accounts of him.

lineage.name: Thomas Corker Sr
lineage.note: Ship's doctor from Co. Meath who settled in Falmouth.

lineage.name: Seniora Doll
lineage.note: Sherbro princess of the house of Ya Kumba.

lineage.name: Robin and Stephen Corker
lineage.note: Inherited their mother's chiefdom and founded the Caulker line.

records.today: Caulker descendants live mainly in Bonthe and Shenge, Sierra Leone; no private living individuals are named here. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Anne Pépin
records.scaleNote: A wealthy signare whose household held enslaved domestic servants and whose family was in the slave trade, per her biography.
records.origins: Born on Gorée to the signare Catherine Baudet and Jean Pépin, a Compagnie des Indes surgeon, she was married à la mode du pays by 14 to Bernard Dupuy.
records.role_summary: She became the richest and most celebrated woman on Gorée, owning several properties and enslaved servants. Her brother Nicolas Pépin built the house now known as the Maison des Esclaves for the family's slave-trading business. In 1786 she became the companion of Governor Stanislas de Boufflers.

roleDetail.d: Richest woman of Gorée in the 1780s–1830s.
Her brother's house served the family's slave-trading business.
Linked with Governor de Boufflers from 1786.

records.legacy: She appears in Maryse Condé's novel 'Segu' and remains an emblem of signare society.

legacyDetail.d: Her family house is tied to the Maison des Esclaves museum on Gorée.

lineage.name: Catherine Baudet and Jean Pépin
lineage.note: A signare and a Company surgeon.

lineage.name: Bernard Dupuy
lineage.note: Her European husband; they had four sons, including René (1773–1820) and Jean (b. 1777).

lineage.name: Nicolas Pépin
lineage.note: Trader who built the Maison des Esclaves house.

lineage.name: Stanislas de Boufflers
lineage.note: French governor of Senegal.

lineage.name: Anna Colas Pépin
lineage.note: Known for her link with the Prince of Joinville.

records.today: No publicly documented living descendants have been traced. Her family is remembered through the Maison des Esclaves on Gorée.

records.name: João I (Nzinga a Nkuwu) of Kongo
records.scaleNote: King when the Portuguese arrived; the Kongo slave trade grew mainly under his son Afonso I.
records.origins: The fifth ManiKongo, he ruled the Kingdom of Kongo when Portuguese navigators arrived in 1483.
records.role_summary: He welcomed Portuguese priests and craftsmen and was baptised as João on 3 May 1491, opening the relationship that soon included trade in captives. He later turned away from Christianity, partly because monogamy conflicted with Kongo's elective, alliance-based kingship.

roleDetail.d: First Kongo king to accept baptism.
His welcome to Portugal set up the trade that his son expanded.

records.legacy: His son Afonso I won the succession in 1509 with Christian support.

legacyDetail.d: His baptism began Kongo's long Christian tradition.

lineage.name: Afonso I
lineage.note: Won the throne in 1509.

records.today: Kongo has no reigning monarch today; Mbanza Kongo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. No individual descendants are named here.

records.name: Karamokho Alfa
records.scaleNote: Founder of Futa Jallon, whose wars and raids became a major source of captives for the Upper Guinea coast; numbers undocumented.
records.origins: A Fula religious leader, son of Alfa Ba, who had called for jihad but died before it began.
records.role_summary: He led the jihad launched around 1726–27 and was chosen head of the new Imamate of Futa Jallon by nine Fulbe scholars. The state's wars and raids supplied captives to coastal traders and enslaved labour for Fulbe farms.

roleDetail.d: First almamy of Futa Jallon.
Futa Jallon's wars supplied captives to the Rio Pongo and Nunez traders.

records.legacy: His descendants formed the Alfaya house, which alternated power with the Soriya house of Ibrahima Sori.

legacyDetail.d: Alfaya and Soriya lineages alternated as almamy until 1896.

lineage.name: Alfa Ba
lineage.note: Called the jihad.

lineage.name: Ibrahima Sori
lineage.note: Military leader of the Soriya house.

records.today: No individual descendants are named here. Present-day descendants carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

events.title: Kongo king baptised
events.text: Nzinga a Nkuwu of Kongo was baptised as João I, opening the Kongo–Portugal alliance that soon included trade in captives.

events.title: Asante defeats Denkyira
events.text: Osei Tutu I's Asante alliance won the Battle of Feyiase, founding the Asante Empire.

events.title: Ghezo's coup in Dahomey
events.text: Ghezo overthrew his brother Adandozan with the help of Francisco Félix de Souza.

events.title: Akitoye signs Lagos treaty
events.text: Restored by British force, Akitoye signed the treaty abolishing the slave trade at Lagos on 1 January 1852.

events.title: Britain exiles King William Dappa Pepple
events.text: The king of Bonny was deposed and exiled by the British; he was restored in 1861.

events.title: Death of Sefu bin Hamid
events.text: Tippu Tip's son was killed fighting the Congo Free State in the Congo Arab war.

events.title: Osei Tutu II enstooled
events.text: Otumfuo Nana Osei Tutu II became the 16th Asantehene, custodian of the Golden Stool.

source.label: Wikipedia — Otumfuo Nana Osei Tutu II

events.title: New king of Dahomey enthroned
events.text: Georges Collinet Béhanzin was enthroned at Abomey as Dada Dèwènondè Gbéhanzin by agreement of the rival royal lineages.

source.label: Benin Web TV — Georges Collinet Béhanzin intronisé

events.title: Last Sultan of Zanzibar dies
events.text: Jamshid bin Abdullah, deposed in the 1964 revolution, died on 30 December 2024.
